claims.text: The proposed intervention is to develop and deploy a neural-network or other machine-learning interatomic potential.
The potential will be trained on extensively sampled ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations representing diverse local environments in the high-temperature liquid.
The trained machine-learning potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap relative to conventional EAM references.
The machine-learning reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 50% relative to EAM references used in TOR-TILD.
The trained machine-learning potential inherently captures many-body interactions.
The trained potential captures the full configurational diversity of the liquid.
Incorporating diverse local configurations from ab initio simulations enables the potential to reproduce the liquid's complex many-body physics.
Reproducing the liquid's many-body physics causes superior overlap with the ab initio target phase space and therefore reduces integration-path mismatch.
The resulting integrated free energies will agree with direct ab initio calculations within ±5 meV/atom.
The intended material domain includes multicomponent HEAs in both solid and liquid states near their high melting temperatures.
The proposed method is applicable to equimolar or near-equimolar CrCoFeNi-based HEAs and similar refractory or transition-metal systems.
The applicable temperature range is close to melting, primarily in the liquid but extending to the adjoining solid.
EAM-based references used in current TOR-TILD implementations inadequately sample the atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid.
EAM-based TOR-TILD references produce larger thermodynamic-integration path mismatches.
The method may lose effectiveness outside the high-temperature liquid regime or for alloy configuration spaces that differ substantially from the training data.
The method's success depends on the quality and breadth of the ab initio training data.
Elemental and binary case studies show improved free-energy predictions from machine-learning potentials.
The estimated 50% mismatch reduction has not been rigorously validated across HEA compositions and temperatures.
